Promises and async/await

A value that isn't ready yet, and the syntax for waiting on it without freezing everything else.

Every controller and service function in the next topic is declared async. Whatever exposure you've had to this in plain JavaScript, it's worth a proper pass now rather than picking it up mid-code — there's no equivalent concept in typical Laravel/PHP work, where a function just runs and returns a value.

A Promise is an object representing a value that doesn't exist yet, but will (or will fail to) at some point — the classic example being "the result of a network request." It can be in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (succeeded, with a value), or rejected (failed, with an error).

fetchTicket(5)
  .then((ticket) => console.log(ticket))   // runs if it fulfills
  .catch((err) => console.error(err));     // runs if it rejects

.then()/.catch() work, but chain awkwardly once you need several asynchronous steps in sequence. async/await is syntax for writing the same thing so it reads like ordinary, top-to-bottom synchronous code:

async function loadTicket(id) {
  const ticket = await fetchTicket(id); // pauses here until it settles
  console.log(ticket);
  return ticket;
}

Two rules that matter for reading the code coming up next:

  • async function always returns a Promise itself — even return 42; inside one actually returns a Promise that resolves to 42, not 42 directly.
  • await only works inside an async function, and only pauses that function — the rest of the program keeps running. That's the "a-" in asynchronous: waiting on one thing never blocks everything else, unlike a synchronous PHP script that stops dead until each line finishes.

A rejected Promise inside an async function behaves like a thrown exception — catchable with an ordinary try/catch wrapped around the await. That detail turns out to matter a lot once these functions are called from Express rather than from other JavaScript — covered properly in this lesson's error-handling topic.
